intro: The Bible is not one kind of book. Open it at random and you might land on a story, a list of laws, a family tree, a poem, a warning from a prophet, a letter to a small church or a vision of beasts rising from the sea. Each of these is a different kind of writing, and each one asks to be read in its own way. This unit teaches the first tool of careful reading: noticing the kind, or genre, before anything else.

In a public school, we read the Bible as literature and history. We ask what the text says, how it is built and how Jewish, Christian and other readers have understood it. We do not ask you to believe it or to reject it. That is why you will hear phrases like 'the text says,' 'tradition names' and 'many scholars think.' Those words keep us accurate about who is speaking.

By the end of the unit you will be able to pick up a passage and tell whether it is narrative, law, genealogy, poetry, prophecy, gospel, letter or apocalypse. You will know what each genre does, what clues give it away and what questions to bring to it. You will also be able to compare a biblical text with an older text from its world, such as the laws of Hammurabi, and say what is alike and what is different.
bigQuestion: How does knowing what kind of writing a passage is change the questions a careful reader asks?

timeline.t: Hammurabi rules Babylon; his law code is carved on a stone found at Susa in 1901
The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, a wisdom text with parallels in Proverbs
David's reign, as tradition dates it; many psalms carry his name
Amos speaks in the northern kingdom of Israel about justice for the poor
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the Temple; Lamentations mourns the city
Persecution under Antiochus IV; many scholars date Daniel's visions to this time
Paul writes 1 Thessalonians, likely the earliest New Testament book
The Gospel of Mark is written, as most scholars date it
Revelation is written to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia
The King James Version is published in England
Abington v. Schempp: the Supreme Court allows study of the Bible as literature in public schools

words.d: the kind of writing a passage is, such as story, law, poem or letter; each kind is read in its own way
writing that tells a story: events in order, with people, places and a plot
a place where a story does not say something the reader wants to know
a direct command with no condition attached, such as 'you shall not steal'
a rule stated as a case: if this happens, then this follows
a list of ancestors and descendants, generation by generation
the pattern in Hebrew poetry where a second line echoes, sharpens or reverses the first
a poem whose lines begin with the letters of the alphabet in order
the opening 'Thus saith the LORD,' which marks a prophet's words as a message from God
one of the four New Testament books about Jesus; the word means good news
a letter; the New Testament holds twenty-one of them
a genre of vision reports about hidden things and the end of history, from a Greek word meaning unveiling

test.q: What is the first question a careful reader of the Bible should ask about a passage?
choices: What kind of writing is it?
test.why: Genre comes first because it tells the reader which questions to bring to the text.

test.q: Which book is mostly law rather than narrative?
test.why: Leviticus is almost all law. Genesis, Ruth and Mark are narrative.

test.q: What did the narrator of 2 Samuel 11 do for most of the chapter about David and Bathsheba?
choices: Reported events without judging until the last verse
test.why: The narrator reports and stays quiet. The single verdict comes at verse 27.

test.q: In Genesis 1, the phrase 'it was good' changes to 'very good' after the sixth day. What reading tool does that illustrate?
choices: Repetition with a change that carries the point
test.why: Repeated phrases guide listeners, and the break in the pattern signals the chapter's climax.

test.q: 'If an ox gore a man and the owner was warned' is an example of what?
test.why: It begins with a condition and states an outcome, which is the shape of case law.

test.q: Why does the Jewish count of the Ten Commandments begin differently from the Protestant count?
choices: Jewish tradition treats 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt' as the first word
The Hebrew text has eleven commandments
test.why: The text gives no numbers. Jewish tradition counts the opening statement about the exodus as the first of the ten.

test.q: What did the Code of Hammurabi and Exodus 21 both address?
choices: An ox that gores a person
test.why: Both codes rule on a goring ox and treat a warned owner as responsible. Their penalties differ.

test.q: What does a genealogy such as Genesis 10 or Matthew 1 do?
choices: Maps who belongs to whom and connects parts of the story
test.why: A genealogy is a map of a people or a family, drawn to make a point about belonging.

test.q: Which sentence uses the habit this unit calls attributing?
choices: Tradition names Moses as the author of the Torah; many scholars think it took shape over centuries.
test.why: Attributing says whose view a statement is, without asserting or denying it.

test.q: Psalm 19:1 says the heavens declare God's glory, and the sky shows God's handiwork. What is this an example of?
test.why: The second line echoes and sharpens the first, which is the basic pattern of Hebrew poetry.

test.q: In the Bible, a prophet is best described as what?
choices: A fortune-teller about the far future
A messenger who speaks to people about their present
test.why: Prophets like Amos delivered messages about what people were doing now and what would follow.

test.q: Which book is a collection of short wise sayings about daily life?
test.why: Proverbs holds two-line sayings about speech, work, anger and friendship. Lamentations mourns Jerusalem.

test.q: What do the Synoptic Gospels have in common?
choices: They all have seven 'I am' sayings
They share many stories in similar words and order
They were all written on Patmos
They were all written by Paul
test.why: Matthew, Mark and Luke can be seen together. John stands apart with its own material.

test.q: Which part of an ancient letter names the sender, the receiver and a wish for well-being?
test.why: The greeting opens the letter, as in 1 Thessalonians 1:1. Thanks, body and farewell follow.

test.q: How do most scholars read the symbols in Revelation?
choices: As a map of events in our own time
As a code the first-century readers understood, pointing to Rome and offering hope
test.why: Most scholars read Revelation first as a message to seven real churches under Roman rule, in symbols they knew.

write.prompt: Pick two passages from this unit that belong to different genres, such as Exodus 21:28–30 and Psalm 19:1, or Amos 5:24 and 1 Thessalonians 1:1. Explain what kind of writing each one is and name two clues that show it. Then tell how the genre changes what a reader asks of the passage, and give one example of how a Jewish, Christian or academic reader has read it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you cite.
Attribute every belief: 'Jewish tradition reads,' 'Christians believe,' 'many scholars think.'
Use the unit's terms, such as parallelism, casuistic law or messenger formula, and explain each one.
Compare readings; do not judge which tradition is right.
Quote only short lines, from the King James Version or the JPS 1917 translation, and say which one.
